name: splitter
intent: Break one composite message into a series of individual messages, each carrying one part of the original, so every part can be routed, processed, retried and scaled on its own while remaining correlatable for later recombination.
problem: A message arrives carrying many elements - an order with line items, a batch document, a multi-record file, a multipart body - and the consumer can only handle one element at a time: the message cannot be routed on data inside it, one bad element poisons the whole batch, one slow element delays all others, and the consumer has to hold the entire composite in memory.
context: Message-based integration where a producer emits composite messages (document messages with repeating records, batch exports, delimited or length-prefixed streams) and downstream endpoints consume homogeneous single-item messages. It applies at ingestion edges, inside a routing chain right after a channel adapter, and to byte streams that must be decoded into frames; whenever the parts are meant to be recombined, the splitter must also add correlation and sequence metadata.
benefits: Each part can be routed on its own content by a Content-Based Router, so an order with items stocked in different systems finally reaches the right endpoint per item.
Failure is isolated: a rejected part goes to the dead-letter channel on its own instead of the whole composite being replayed, and remaining parts still complete.
Parts process in parallel and across competing consumers, so throughput scales with consumer count instead of with the size of the composite.
Peak memory and message size drop: a streaming splitter emits parts while reading, which keeps a payload under broker limits and lets processing start before the composite has been fully read.
Downstream endpoints stay single-item consumers, so existing channels, handlers and validation code are reused unchanged - the splitter absorbs the impedance mismatch in one place.
tradeoffs: Message count explodes: one composite becomes N messages, multiplying broker traffic, storage, serialisation and per-message overhead (Kafka/SQS/cloud pricing included).
Ordering is no longer implied - parallel processing scrambles parts, so order-sensitive consumers need sequence numbers plus a Resequencer.

Atomicity is lost by construction: the composite's transaction boundary does not survive the split, so partial completion is the normal case and the design needs idempotent consumers and compensation.
Split metadata is mandatory overhead: without correlation id and sequence number/size the parts cannot be recombined or even counted, and the leftovers are silently lost.
The split logic is coupled to the payload format (XPath, JSON path, MIME boundary, delimiter), so a producer format change breaks the splitter rather than a mapper.
Fragments are often meaningless alone - a header or total belongs to the composite - which pushes context duplication or an enrichment step into the parts.
End-to-end observability fragments: one logical flow becomes many messages, so tracing, metrics and debugging need correlation-aware tooling to stay coherent.

participants.responsibility: Consumes one composite message, determines the part boundary (repeating element, delimiter, length prefix, schema node), and emits one derived message per part on its output channel.
The inbound message whose body holds multiple elements - a collection, a document with repeated records, or a delimited byte stream.
A derived message carrying exactly one element of the composite plus the headers it needs to be processed as a standalone message.
Correlation identifier, sequence number and sequence size (with a completion marker when the size is unknowable in advance) that keep parts traceable and re-combinable.
Transports the parts to their next stage - typically a Datatype Channel, a Content-Based Router, or the input side of an Aggregator.
Optional destination for an input whose split produced no parts, so an empty result is visible instead of silently dropped.

use_cases: Order intake: an order document with many line items is split so each item is routed to the inventory or fulfilment system that owns it (the originating catalog's own example).
Batch ingestion: a nightly CSV/XML export is split into one message per record so records can be processed in parallel and retried individually.
Oversized payloads: a large document or multipart body is split to stay under broker message-size limits, with each part carrying its own header block.
Stream framing at an ingestion edge: an inbound byte stream is decoded into frames, one message per record, so processing starts before the whole stream has arrived.
Fan-out by element type: parts are split and then routed to different endpoints, turning a monolithic consumer into several specialised ones.
Bulk APIs: a partner system only offers a batch endpoint, so the batch is split into per-item messages for the internal event-driven flow.

Apache Camel Split EIP: <split> or .split() breaks an exchange body (list, array, Iterable, delimited string) into sub-exchanges with streaming mode to bound memory and parallelProcessing to run parts concurrently, optionally grouped back via an AggregationStrategy.

Spring Integration Splitter: the Splitter EIP turns an Iterable, Iterator, array, Stream or reactive Publisher payload into one message per element and auto-populates CORRELATION_ID, SEQUENCE_NUMBER and SEQUENCE_SIZE headers; iterator splits report SEQUENCE_SIZE 0, so a downstream aggregator needs a custom release strategy.

AWS Step Functions Map state: a workflow fans an array input (inline mode) or an S3 CSV/JSON/object-list (distributed mode, up to 10,000 child-workflow executions) out to one iteration per item, with MaxConcurrency bounding the fan-out and results recombined by the Map state.
avoid_when: The message already carries a single item - a plain handler or a Message Translator is the whole solution, no splitter needed.
All elements must be processed atomically as one unit (an aggregate whose invariants span the whole document): keep it whole for a single consumer, or move the bulk out of band with Claim Check.
A downstream partner expects the document shape - split it nowhere; translate or window it instead (Message Translator, Legacy Window).
The producer is under your control: emitting one message per element at the source is cheaper and more robust than splitting after the composite has crossed the broker.
Only a subset of the elements is wanted: Message Filter (content filter) selects without fanning out.
Order must be preserved end to end and no resequencer exists: a single-threaded consumer of the whole composite is simpler than split plus reorder.
anti_patterns: "Split and forget": emitting N parts with no correlation id or sequence metadata, so nothing can be recombined and partial results are invisible.
Splitter-as-transformer: the splitter also enriches, validates or routes each part, so a payload format change forces a rewrite of the routing logic.
Unbounded fan-out: splitting a million-record file into a million broker messages without back-pressure, batching or throttling.
Splitting after the broker: fanning out inside the consumer loop once the composite has already been transported and stored.
Split-then-aggregate for a payload that never needed splitting, paying two components and lost atomicity for nothing.
Silent partial publication: swallowing split errors and emitting the subset that could be built as if the composite had been processed.
design_principles: Single responsibility: the splitter decides part boundaries and nothing else - routing, translation and aggregation stay in their own patterns.
Separation of concerns: knowledge of the composite's structure stays at the integration edge instead of leaking into every consumer.
Make flow control explicit: correlation and sequence metadata turn recombination from guesswork into a declarative contract (Correlation Identifier, Message Sequence).
Composition over monoliths: split is one stage of a pipelines-and-filters chain (split -> route -> process -> aggregate).
Fail loudly: every part is accounted for through a size or completion marker, so partial results are detectable rather than assumed complete.
Open/closed: the boundary rule is a parameter or expression, so new payload shapes do not require edits to existing consumers.
best_practices: Split as close to the source as possible - at the producer or the ingestion channel adapter - so the composite never travels through the messaging infrastructure.
Always attach a correlation id plus sequence number and size (or a completion marker when the size is unknowable) before the first part is published.
Keep the splitter stateless and deterministic; recombination state belongs to the Aggregator.
Emit parts lazily (iterator, generator, stream, chunk iterator) and let back-pressure pace the fan-out instead of materialising all parts.
Retain the original composite (or a Claim Check reference) so a failed split can be replayed and audited.
Handle the empty split explicitly on a discard or invalid-message channel rather than publishing nothing.
Make each part self-describing: copy the relevant headers, include the owning element's identity, and keep the payload free of references to the composite.
Bound the fan-out and make consumers idempotent, because parts may be redelivered independently.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Splitter (Message Routing chapter), with Aggregator as its recombining counterpart.
